newsitem.title: USA: Vandalism halts Habitat for Humanity projects.
newsitem.headline: Vandalism halts Habitat for Humanity projects.

text.p: A wave of vandalism has scuttled homebuilding projects by the state's oldest chapter of low-income builder Habitat for Humanity, officials said on Thursday.

The most recent acts occurred last weekend when a cluster of homes under construction were ravaged. Vandals struck on Friday and Saturday afternoons, shortly after workers finished for the day, they said.
Windows were broken, walls punctured, paint was poured on carpet. The floors were flooded when the vandals left the faucets running.
"The community is in an outrage over this," said Della Dove, the executive director of the Sea Island chapter of Habitat for Humanity. "This just hurts us to the core."

Last Easter, $1,500 in building materials was stolen from other Habitat houses being built in the same neighbourhood. When it is finished, the Island Estates subdivision will include 24 Habitat homes.

Habitat for Humanity, a worldwide organisation based in Georgia, builds homes for low-income people who would not otherwise qualify for a home loan. Much of the labour for such projects was donated, cutting the average cost of a home to $35,000, but the fair market value is more like $65,000.
Payments usually run from $200 to $250 a month. Habitat sells the houses at no profit and finances with no interest. Since 1976 the group has built 55,000 houses worldwide, with 1,200 chapters.
In Charleston, the nearest mainland city to the island, police were investigating the vandalism.
